practice.title: Remembering Death to Purify and Practice Purely
agreedSteps: Remember death throughout the week — use it to fuel both purification and the aspiration to practice Dharma purely, without worldly concerns.
Try purifying one worldly concern each morning — resources, pleasure, reputation, or praise — targeting a different one each day as a focused purification practice.
steps: Check resistance to impermanence and change. Notice where the mind tries to freeze things in place out of comfort, insecurity, or attachment — and recognize that everything is in constant flux.

Work with the three points of death meditation as a package: I will definitely die, the time of death is uncertain, and only Dharma can help me. If the meditation feels flat, return to the first point — 'I will definitely die' — which is often underdeveloped.

Examine the degree to which Dharma practice is motivated by worldly concerns. Ask: am I meditating just to feel good right now? Try to shift intention even slightly toward benefiting others or future lives — each small shift makes the practice less impure.
When virtue feels hard and non-virtue feels easy, use that as proof of the karmic burden from holding wrong views in the past — fuel for purification, not low self-esteem.
practice.quote: Therefore, in the beginning, our immediate aspiration should not be to gain the perfect results of Dharma practice. Rather, it should be to practice purely.

commentary.title: Holding Wrong Views vs. Ignorance
content: The actual action of holding wrong views has to be a complete action. It doesn't just mean being ignorant. We are all ignorant. If ignorance were the same as holding wrong views, there would be no way to leave samsara, because we'd be creating the most heinous negative action over and over until the end of time. Ignorance itself doesn't create negativity — it just means not knowing. It's what we do next that creates the negativity.

The complete action of holding wrong views is actively denying Dharma, very purposefully. Not just failing to act in accordance with it — those are two different things. Holding a wrong view would be saying anger is justified and right and good, and anyone who says otherwise is an idiot. Once we become a Buddhist, it's hard to fully create this action again. If we had no interest in Buddhist truths at all, we probably wouldn't come to TTP.

But we have held these views billions of times in the past, and that karma ripens as disinterest in Dharma, confusion, frustration, or no spiritual experience in meditation. Every time meditation doesn't go according to plan, it helps to remember this as a root cause. It gets us out of low self-esteem thinking — it's not that I'm bad at this. It's just karma from holding wrong views ripening. And all that should do is motivate us to purify more.

commentary.title: The Four Factors of Non-Virtue
content: The difference between great and small non-virtue is determined by four factors: object, time, action, and mind. The heaviest karma is incurred when the object is venerable, when the action occurs on days of spiritual observance, when harm is inflicted slowly rather than swiftly, and when the mind is strongly motivated by anger and rejoices in harm.

The practical application comes down to mindfulness and intention. On days of spiritual observance, we should be extra careful. We can cultivate an attitude of respect toward all beings. And at the heart of it: stop overthinking the results of everything we do. Go into an inquiry — what's my intention? What's driving me? Where am I really coming from? Intention is the crème de la crème of all this. If we hurt somebody without an intention to hurt them, it's not a completed action. It has to start with that negative intention.

commentary.title: Gratitude for Parents
content: Our parents could have had an abortion — which means we are not here. Every parent who did not do that is kind. Having someone live in your body, putting your life on hold for nine months, going through the ordeal of childbirth — that's incredibly generous. It's a bit of a cop-out to just blame our parents for all our problems. It's very easy to do, but often it's a spoiled thing to do. It's our karma, not our parents.

Our practice of seeing all living beings as a mother and developing gratitude for all living beings is contingent specifically on having gratitude for our own mother and father, even with their incredible imperfection. When we love someone deeply, we're patient with them. So when we're getting annoyed, we've forgotten our love. We should also meditate on the death of our parents — they will die, and they might die today. Sometimes that moves our heart in a way that changes how we think about them.

commentary.title: Death and Pure Practice
content: If we can develop equanimity with regard to the concerns of this life, our practice becomes pure. 'Pure' means not motivated by the eight worldly concerns — attachment to resources, pleasure, reputation, and praise. In the beginning, our immediate aspiration should not be to gain the perfect results of Dharma practice. Rather, it should be to practice purely. If we're ambitious to experience results, that ambition is an obstacle because it's mixed with attachment to worldly concerns.

When we don't practice purely, we make a lot of mistakes — both in personal practice and in teaching. If we're teaching for praise, we do things to get praised rather than teaching Dharma correctly. Or we second-guess ourselves when the praise doesn't come. One Dharma teacher friend shared that when he stopped trying to control his center's success and committed to teaching pure Dharma only, the center flourished. The contaminated intention was replaced by an aligned Dharma intention, and blessings and inspirations started to flow.
This isn't an instant fix. We have to wean off the worldly concerns one at a time. But this all leads us into thinking about death more and more — death meditation is what helps us practice purely.

commentary.title: The Nine Rounds of Death Meditation
content: Traditionally there are three main points in meditation on death, each with three sub-points — nine points total. Point one: I will definitely die. Point two: the time of death is uncertain. Point three: only Dharma can help me. It's actually a five-point package if you include the faults of not remembering death and the benefits of remembering death.

Many people skip right to 'I may die today' without having fully internalized 'I will definitely die.' The meditation then feels flat, because that second point doesn't make sense without the first. If we haven't found absolute vigor and love for meditation on death, it's a sign that the first part is missing. One student recently said he does it every morning and it feels like it solves every problem. He found the meaning of meditation on death.

The third point gives the meditation a virtuous outlet. Without it, 'I may die today' has no clear direction. But when it flows into 'therefore only Dharma can protect me,' it becomes fuel. At the time of death, our wealth can't help us. Our friends and relatives can't help us. Even our own body is of no use — the First Panchen Lama said: the body that we've cherished for so long cheats us at the time when we need it the most.
commentary.quote: For the skillful Dharma practitioner, the thought 'I may die today' flows into 'therefore only Dharma can protect me.' For an ordinary person, it's just manure with no outlet. For a farmer, it's a gift.

commentary.title: Correct Reasoning vs. Probabilistic Thinking
content: In Buddhist practice, we have a very strict standard for something being logical — syllogistic reasoning with three modes: the property of the subject, forward pervasion, and reverse pervasion. Most of our modern thinking doesn't operate by these standards. It's either probabilistic thinking (which is a good-enough guess, not a cause) or just outsourced to experts of our choice.

Probabilistic thinking is useful for predicting better and better, but it doesn't provide precision understanding of what's going on. As Buddhists, we're trying to understand precisely what leads to what. The example from MTB: 'the hell realms don't exist because I can't see them' — that's not good logic. It means anything I can't see doesn't exist, and things I do see do exist. Both are false.

If we can strip our mind of all the conclusions that aren't built up from logical analysis — wipe the slate clean of things relied upon via random experts or guesses or things learned from parents — we'll see the Dharma start to shine very brightly. We'll see that the teachings of Buddha are all logically sound, and that anything people say to contradict Buddha is not.

commentary.title: Suffering Is Not Purification
content: Even if we have chronic problems, pain, or a lot of difficulty, it doesn't mean we shouldn't overtly do a purification practice. Those are two different things. When we're encountering pain or difficulty, we can purify it by happily accepting it, regarding it as arising from our past negative karma. If we're deeply, happily accepting, then it is a very powerful purification practice. But just experiencing suffering and pain has nothing to do with purification.

Sometimes people say colloquially, 'I'm purifying a lot' — meaning I'm suffering a lot. That's not correct. We have to be happily accepting, thinking, 'I'm regarding this as purifying my negative karma.' Without that transformation, we might actually be making the karma worse — because we could be suffering with a lot of anger and creating even more negative karma. Just by suffering doesn't make us a Buddha. Suffering and transforming it to the spiritual path makes us into a Buddha.

commentary.title: Karmic Patterns as Gifts
content: When someone problematic appears in our life and we notice they're just like someone from our past, that recognition is incredibly valuable. It's our chance to purify the way we treated the person before. With the mind of purification in our practice repertoire, these bad things genuinely feel like gifts from the Buddhas.

Certain kinds of people and things that rile us up often repeat in different bodies over and over again until we get the message. It just keeps coming. And then when we get the message, it just goes away — they disappear, or the people who are like them. Then other people show up that test our other karmic issues. When we notice these patterns, we can approach them in a much lighter way. We're not stuck. We're creative, open, looking at it from all sorts of angles.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Working on purifying holding wrong views — recognized that poor concentration comes from past wrong views, and that she not only held wrong views but taught them to others and was excited when they adopted them. In the break, practiced noticing wrong views, identifying correct views, and rejoicing in them. Also used procrastination as a mirror for death awareness: if she died right now, the purity of her mind is the big thing that would be left undone.

dataShares.speaker: Suzanne
dataShares.summary: Had always felt she didn't need to purify because of the suffering from her chronic illness, but experimented with doing it anyway. Some turbulence followed but then settled. Also gave two small Tara statues with mantras to her sister and a friend going through chemo — a lovely experience of the mind of giving.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.summary: A problematic person appeared in his life. Recognized the person was just like someone from his past and felt this was an opportunity to purify how he treated the person before. Felt the person was a gift from the Buddhas. The mind of purification made what would have been a bad experience feel transformative.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.summary: Spent the week with in-laws — an annual tradition that serves as a Petri dish for practice. Routine was disrupted and practice was harder away from the center. Tried regarding all virtuous actions as purifying. Noticed the in-laws were more harmonious than ever after years of praying for them — an encouragement toward the long game of practice without expecting quick results.
